entries.title: Development and validation of a measure of work decision styles
entries.summary: Four studies developed a 20-item measure of analytical, intuitive, collaborative, and decisive work decision styles. Validation included factor analysis, item response theory, and associations with self-reported job performance.
entries.why_it_matters: The measure could support research into decision-making and development needs at work. Its relationship with performance needs further testing against outcomes beyond self-reports.

entries.title: Work engagement and mental well-being in the ICT age: investigating the role of job resources among white-collar workers in Europe
entries.summary: An analysis of 20,347 white-collar workers across 36 countries found that opportunities to demonstrate competence were strongly associated with engagement, while trust and cooperation were important predictors of mental well-being.
entries.why_it_matters: Employee surveys and work-design reviews could measure opportunities to use skills and team cooperation alongside technology use. The observational findings do not establish that changing those resources will improve outcomes.

entries.title: Workplace AI Trust: Scale Development, Preliminary Psychometric Validation, and Associations with Employee AI Experience
entries.summary: Researchers developed an eight-item workplace AI trust scale using a survey of Polish working adults. The items showed internal consistency, but model fit and evidence for comparisons between groups were mixed.
entries.why_it_matters: The scale offers candidate questions for research into employee AI experience. Practitioners should validate it locally before comparing groups or using scores to guide consequential decisions.

entries.title: Conservation in place: perceived pay inequity as a chronic occupational stressor in a high-unemployment labor market
entries.summary: A secondary analysis of interviews with ten employees and managers at one South African consumer-goods organization examined responses to perceived pay unfairness. Some participants described remaining in their jobs while reducing discretionary effort.
entries.why_it_matters: The findings suggest pairing retention metrics with confidential measures of perceived pay fairness and employee voice. The small, single-organization study cannot estimate how widespread these responses are.

entries.title: Exploring the ambivalence of job autonomy in agile work context: A qualitative study
entries.summary: Interviews with 20 employees in one agile organization found that participants valued autonomy but also described constraints and demands associated with self-organization and responsibility.
entries.why_it_matters: Work-design assessments could distinguish advertised autonomy from employees’ experienced discretion, support, and workload. The interviews provide context for survey design rather than evidence of effects across organizations.

entries.title: Role uncertainty in AI-enabled organizational change: linking perceived AI adoption to job stress
entries.summary: A three-wave survey of 355 employees in Japanese organizations found that perceived AI adoption was associated with greater role ambiguity and subsequent job stress. The association between adoption and ambiguity was weaker where change communication was rated more highly.
entries.why_it_matters: When evaluating an AI rollout, measure role clarity and change communication alongside stress. The observational design does not establish that communication caused the difference.

entries.title: How Safety Incident Reporting Decisions Are Made: A Multilevel, Process-Oriented Perspective
entries.summary: Interviews with 34 shipbuilding and ship-repair employees examined how they decide whether to report safety incidents. Reasons for reporting and not reporting were not simply opposites, and workers described interacting personal, organizational and economic considerations.
entries.why_it_matters: Incident counts alone can miss reporting barriers. Safety teams could supplement them with confidential interviews about the effort, perceived consequences and practical constraints involved in reporting.

entries.title: Mental distress diverges by gender across the transition to first parenthood and is not consistently buffered by working from home
entries.summary: A UK household-panel event study found differing distress trajectories for employed women and men after first parenthood, but no consistent evidence that working from home beforehand buffered those trajectories. Results for mothers were affected by selection into continued employment, and remote-work estimates were imprecise.
entries.why_it_matters: When assessing support for new parents, track well-being and employment exits rather than assuming remote work is sufficient. Interpret gender comparisons cautiously when leave and workforce exits affect who remains observable.

entries.title: Associations between digital and automated work and psychosocial outcomes: Cross-sectional results from the Gutenberg Health Study
entries.source: International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health
entries.summary: In a cross-sectional German study of 5,730 participants, digital work had mixed associations with job satisfaction, engagement and intentions to leave, while automated work was associated with higher burnout and lower satisfaction. Technical and skill-related demands were also associated with several adverse outcomes.
entries.why_it_matters: Workforce surveys can distinguish digital work, automation, technology-related demands and employees’ experiences instead of treating technology exposure as one measure. The associations do not establish that technology caused the outcomes.

entries.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
entries.summary: This preprint models how choosing between independent work and AI answers could affect skill acquisition and retention over repeated tasks. Under its assumptions, incentives for independent practice can help sustain skill even when AI-assisted task accuracy remains high.
entries.why_it_matters: The model can inform decisions about protected practice time and how to measure skill retention during AI deployment. Its predictions need empirical testing before being treated as evidence of workplace effects.

entries.title: Uncovering the Mechanisms of Policy Interventions: A Difference-In-Differences Framework for Mediation Analysis
entries.summary: The authors develop a difference-in-differences framework for studying how HR interventions affect outcomes through intermediate mechanisms. The method accommodates some unobserved confounding but requires assumptions about untreated trends and changes over time.
entries.why_it_matters: People analytics teams evaluating a training rollout could use the framework to examine whether skill acquisition helps explain performance changes, while making the required causal assumptions explicit.

entries.title: The Organizational Benefits of Neurodiversity: A Strategic Human Capital–Based Systematic Review and Research Agenda
entries.summary: A systematic review of 88 studies examines how HR research has approached the organizational benefits of neurodiversity. It finds that evidence on organization-level outcomes remains limited and uneven.
entries.why_it_matters: Teams evaluating neuroinclusive hiring or workplace adjustments can use the review to plan measures of implementation and outcomes without assuming that organizational benefits are already established.

entries.title: Watched by the algorithm: algorithmic monitoring, worker resistance and well-being in the gig economy
entries.summary: A three-wave survey of 224 gig workers in Pakistan linked perceived algorithmic monitoring with worker resistance, while an experiment with 115 participants examined monitoring and fairness together. Resistance patterns in the experiment did not always match the researchers’ predictions.
entries.why_it_matters: Organizations assessing worker-monitoring systems could measure perceived fairness and resistance alongside well-being rather than relying on productivity indicators alone.

entries.title: The fluid emergence of GenAI roles in temporary teams: How teams calibrate delegation under shifting situational demands
entries.summary: Interviews with 28 teams during a 48-hour innovation sprint identified different roles that generative AI assumed as teams moved between tasks. Each role presented distinct opportunities and risks, including trivial advice and excessive reliance.
entries.why_it_matters: Managers designing AI-assisted teamwork can specify which tasks may be delegated, what output is expected, and who reviews it at each stage of a project.

entries.title: The new meaning of office: how hybrid work changes formal organizational structure from a place perspective
entries.summary: Across 49 interviews in two international organizations, researchers observed changes in how HR positions were grouped and centralized alongside shifts toward hybrid work. Employees also described the office as a place for social connection.
entries.why_it_matters: When reviewing a hybrid-work policy, people teams could track changes in reporting lines and collaboration alongside office attendance, rather than treating attendance as a sufficient measure of organizational impact.
